In brief

Parody. "When, lo, there came about them all a great brightness and they beheld the chariot wherein He stood ascend to heaven [...] at an angle of fortyfive degrees over Donohoe's in Little Green street like a shot off a shovel": in the last of 33 parodies Bloom rolls away on his carriage not as a foreign monarch taking leave of Ireland but as a great prophet taking leave of the earth, and Joyce's prose imitates, for the first time, the sonorous cadences and primal images of the Judeo-Christian Bible.

At more length

A paper handout seen in Lestrygonians and again in Wandering Rocks declares that "Elijah is coming," echoing the prophecy in the book of Malachi that the prophet will return before the Day of Judgment to announce the coming of the Messiah. At the end of Cyclops it appears that Elijah has indeed come. And gone. The jaunting car in which Bloom is riding becomes a chariot taking him up to heaven, just as Elijah in the book of Kings was taken up to heaven while still alive.

The emphasis on Bloom's "great brightness"—a word used three times in five sentences—involves recollection of several different biblical passages. One is the moment in 2 Kings when Elijah, walking with his disciple Elisha, finds a fiery chariot waiting for him: "And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire" (2.11). Elijah makes a posthumous appearance in the gospel of Matthew, again in the context of great brightness: "And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias [Elijah] talking with him (17:1-3). In a clear allusion to this Transfiguration, Bloom is "clothed upon in the glory of the brightness, having raiment as of the sun." But he is also "fair as the moon and terrible that for awe they durst not look upon Him," precisely echoing a verse in the Song of Solomon: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" (6:10).

Joyce also echoes a motif found in two of these biblical passages: dialogue between those on the earth and a heavenly Father. When Elisha sees his master whirling up to heaven in a fiery cloud he cries, "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more" (2 Kings 2:12). He appears to be addressing Elijah, not God, but the two possibilities do not seem to entirely exclude one another. After Peter, James, and John have witnessed Jesus's transfiguration, "a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 17:5). In the parody "there came a voice out of heaven, calling: Elijah! Elijah! And He answered with a main cry: Abba! Adonai!" Abba is Hebrew (originally Aramaic) for Father, and Adonai is Hebrew for Lord. Bloom, then, is answering a call to return to his heavenly maker.

The hilarious extravagance of honoring the humble, atheistical Bloom with a transfiguration and near-apotheosis is deflated by some down-to-earth language in the parody's final half-sentence. Scientific exactitude and geographic specificity return in the disclosure that Bloom was launched into eternity "at an angle of fortyfive degrees over Donohoe's in Little Green street," making him seem less a mythical figure than a circus performer shot out of a cannon. The concluding simile of his flying by "like a shot off a shovel" adds some earthy agricultural associations, as if he is a peat clod or cow pie tossed out of the way by an energetic farmer. Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that this American expression means "very fast"—one would wish for one's prophets to rise majestically rather explosively—and that, according to Ellmann's biography, it was one of John Stanislaus Joyce's favorite sayings. Joyce alternates hyperbole and bathos throughout Cyclops, but never more memorably than here.

John Hunt 2026
